elements.quote: A systematic review and meta-analysis was therefore conducted
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly identifies the work as a systematic review (and meta-analysis).

elements.quote: Purpose The effect of systemic hemostatic agents initiated during pre-hospital care of severely injured patients with ongoing bleeding or traumatic brain injury (TBI) remains controversial.
elements.reason: The abstract provides the stated purpose/review question regarding effectiveness and safety in the specified patient setting.

elements.quote: Methods PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Library databases were searched up to October 2021 for studies that investigated pre-hospital initiated treatment with systemic hemostatic agents.
elements.reason: The abstract indicates what kinds of studies were searched (systemic hemostatic agents in pre-hospital initiated treatment) but does not clearly specify the main inclusion and exclusion criteria.

elements.quote: Methods PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Library databases were searched up to October 2021
elements.reason: The abstract reports the information sources (PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library) and the search time limit (up to October 2021).

elements.quote: The certainty of evidence was evaluated with the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation approach, and the quality of each study was determined with the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the method used for assessing risk of bias/quality of included studies (Cochrane risk-of-bias tool).

elements.quote: Results Five trials of tranexamic acid (TXA) met the inclusion criteria for this meta-analysis.
elements.reason: The abstract states that a meta-analysis was conducted but does not report detailed methods for presenting and synthesizing results (e.g., pooling approach).

elements.quote: Results Five trials of tranexamic acid (TXA) met the inclusion criteria for this meta-analysis.
elements.reason: The abstract gives the number of included trials but does not report the total number of included participants or summarize participant characteristics.

elements.quote: With a high certainty of evidence, when compared to placebo TXA reduced mortality at 24 h (relative risk = 0.83, 95% confidence interval = 0.73-0.94) and at 1 month among trauma patients (0.91, 0.85-0.97).
elements.reason: Main outcome results are provided with effect estimates and confidence intervals, but the abstract does not include the total number of included studies/participants per outcome.

elements.quote: TXA reduced mortality at 24 h (relative risk = 0.83, 95% confidence interval = 0.73-0.94) and at 1 month among trauma patients (0.91, 0.85-0.97).
elements.reason: Because a meta-analysis is reported, the abstract provides the summary estimate (relative risk) and its 95% confidence intervals.

elements.quote: when compared to placebo TXA reduced mortality at 24 h ... and at 1 month
elements.reason: The abstract compares TXA versus placebo and indicates the direction of effect (TXA favors lower mortality).
The abstract does not briefly summarize important limitations of the included evidence (e.g., risk of bias, inconsistency, or imprecision) as required by this criterion.

elements.quote: Conclusion Balancing benefits and harms, TXA initiated in the pre-hospital setting can be used for patients experiencing major trauma with significant hemorrhage since it reduces the risk of mortality at 24 h and one month with no difference in terms of adverse effects when compared to placebo.
elements.reason: The abstract provides a general interpretation of findings and implications for use in the stated patient group.
No primary funding source for the review is reported in the provided abstract text.
The abstract text provided does not report any study registration information (register name and registration number).

elements.quote: Purpose The effect of systemic hemostatic agents initiated during pre-hospital care of severely injured patients with ongoing bleeding or traumatic brain injury (TBI) remains controversial.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the current state of knowledge by stating the effects “remains controversial,” indicating existing uncertainty.

elements.quote: A systematic review and meta-analysis was therefore conducted to assess the effectiveness and safety of systemic hemostatic agents as an adjunctive therapy in people with major trauma and hemorrhage or TBI in the context of developing the Italian National Institute of Health guidelines on major trauma integrated management.
elements.reason: It explicitly explains the importance/need for conducting the review (to assess effectiveness and safety and to inform guideline development).

elements.quote: Our results are in agreement with those in the current scientific literature. Specifically, meta-analyses and systematic reviews conducted in the pre-hospital or the hospital setting found that TXA reduces the risk of death from all causes by about 20% [44, 53, 54] and less hemorrhagic expansion [44] among TBI patients [32, 46]; yet some results were discrepant with respect to functional status [32, 44, 54, 55].
elements.reason: The evidence discusses existing (systematic review/meta-analysis) findings and notes discrepancies, but it does not clearly explain the need for the current review in relation to those specific prior systematic reviews (e.g., an explicit “therefore we conducted this review” tied to prior reviews/updates/replications).

elements.quote: The treatment benefit is time-dependent, the benefits of TXA therapy seen in the first 3 h may be explained by the increasing levels of plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 and a reduction in fibrinolysis.
elements.reason: For the intervention effects, the manuscript briefly provides a mechanism/biological rationale (PAI-1 increase and reduced fibrinolysis) explaining the treatment benefit.
No logic model or hypothesised relationships between intervention components and outcomes are described in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: This systematic review aimed to assess the effectiveness and safety of systemic hemostatic agents as adjunctive treatment measures initiated in the pre-hospital setting and then continued in the in-hospital setting in patients with major trauma and hemorrhage or with TBI.
elements.reason: The objective of the review is stated (assess effectiveness and safety), but the evidence does not show that the objective(s) or question(s) are explicitly formulated using a relevant question-formulation framework.

elements.quote: Two independent authors (A.B. and G.P.) completed reference screening and study selection using the following predefined inclusion criteria: (1) population : children, young people, or adults who have experienced a suspected hemorrhage or TBI following a traumatic incident; (2) intervention : administration of a systemic hemostatic agent, (e.g., rFVIIa, TXA, fibrinogen concentrate, prothrombin complex concentrate, or another anti-fibrinolytic agent); (3) comparison : no treatment, placebo, standard care (e.g., crystalloids, blood components), or any other hemostatic agent; and (iv) setting: systemic hemostatic treatment initiated in the prehospital setting.
elements.reason: Planned comparisons consistent with a PICO/variant structure (population, intervention, comparison, setting) are described for eligibility criteria, but the evidence does not indicate that these comparisons are stated specifically as part of the review objectives/question formulation using PICO (it appears within inclusion criteria rather than an explicit planned-comparisons statement in the objectives).

elements.quote: Two independent authors (A.B. and G.P.) completed reference screening and study selection using the following predefined inclusion criteria: (1) population : children, young people, or adults who have experienced a suspected hemorrhage or TBI following a traumatic incident; (2) intervention : administration of a systemic hemostatic agent, (e.g., rFVIIa, TXA, fibrinogen concentrate, prothrombin complex concentrate, or another anti-fibrinolytic agent); (3) comparison : no treatment, placebo, standard care (e.g., crystalloids, blood components), or any other hemostatic agent; and (iv) setting: systemic hemostatic treatment initiated in the prehospital setting. Only RCTs were considered eligible for inclusion; case reports, editorials, and letters were excluded from the search.
elements.reason: The review specifies framework components (population, intervention, comparison, setting) and eligible study design (RCTs only). However, follow-up requirements are not explicitly specified in the retrieved evidence.
The retrieved evidence does not specify eligibility criteria related to report characteristics such as dissemination year, language, or publication/report status.
No distinction is reported between exclusions because outcomes were not measured versus exclusions because outcome results were not reported.
The retrieved evidence does not specify the groups used in each synthesis or link them to the comparisons defined in the review objectives.
Although inclusion is restricted to RCTs, the retrieved evidence does not provide rationales for notable eligibility restrictions.

elements.quote: Two professional librarians searched the Embase, PubMed (Medline), and the Cochrane Library databases for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) published up to October 12, 2021
elements.reason: The date up to which the information sources (databases) were searched is reported as “published up to October 12, 2021.”

elements.quote: Two professional librarians searched the Embase, PubMed (Medline), and the Cochrane Library databases for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) published up to October 12, 2021
elements.reason: Database names are reported (Embase, PubMed/Medline, Cochrane Library) and a cutoff date is given, but the search interface/platform and available coverage dates are not reported.

elements.quote: In addition, six references were sourced from ClinicalTrials.gov [35-40].
elements.reason: A study register/online repository is named (ClinicalTrials.gov), but its date restrictions are not provided.
The evidence does not report specific websites/search engines/online sources (with names and URLs) besides ClinicalTrials.gov, and no URLs are provided.
No organisations or manufacturers contacted to identify studies are named in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: Authors were contacted if the reported data were insufficient or unclear.
elements.reason: The type of individuals contacted (authors) is described, but the evidence does not provide broader details about the types of individuals contacted specifically to identify studies.
The evidence does not specify any types of reference lists examined.
The evidence does not describe backward or forward citation searching (seed reports/citation platform and search date).
The evidence does not report journals or conference proceedings consulted, their date coverage, or search methods.

elements.quote: Full details of the search strategy are reported in Supplemental Material 2.
elements.reason: The manuscript indicates that the full search strategies are available in Supplemental Material 2, but the retrieved evidence does not provide the complete, database-by-database search strategies as actually run.
No retrieved evidence reports search limits or describes how limits were justified by reference to eligibility criteria.

elements.quote: Following the GRADE-ADOLOPMENT development process [19], the search strategy included in the high-quality NICE guideline on major trauma from 2015 [20] has been updated.
elements.reason: A published search approach (from the NICE guideline) is cited and indicates an update, but the retrieved evidence does not describe the specific adaptations to the search.
No retrieved evidence specifies any natural-language processing or text-analysis tools used to refine search terms.
No retrieved evidence specifies tools used to translate search strings between sources.
No retrieved evidence describes any validation of the search strategy or validation process/studies.
No retrieved evidence describes any peer review of the search strategy (including any tool/process such as PRESS).

The retrieved evidence does not indicate that the search structure was not based on PICO; instead, the manuscript states which databases were searched and that full details are in Supplemental Material 2.

elements.quote: Two independent authors (A.B. and G.P.) completed reference screening and study selection using the following predefined inclusion criteria:
elements.reason: Reports that two authors screened records and completed study selection, but does not specify the number of reviewers screening each distinct stage (e.g., screening vs full-text eligibility) for full reports.

elements.quote: Two independent authors (A.B. and G.P.) completed reference screening and study selection
elements.reason: Explicitly states the authors worked independently.

elements.quote: Discrepancies between reviewers were resolved by consulting a third author (O.C.).
elements.reason: Describes the process for resolving disagreements (consulting a third author).
No description was provided of processes used to obtain or confirm eligibility information from study investigators.
No methods are reported for translating abstracts or full articles for eligibility assessment.
No information is reported on integration of automation tools into the selection process.
No externally derived classifiers (with version/reference), or record removal prior to screening, are described.
No internally derived classifiers, training, or validation are described.
No machine-learning prioritisation tools or screening stopping/prioritisation rules are described.
No crowdsourcing platforms or their integration into study selection are described.
No previously screened datasets used to eliminate records are described.

elements.quote: Two independent authors (A.B. and G.P.) extracted data on publication year, country, and characteristics of the study population ...
elements.reason: The manuscript reports the number of reviewers/data collectors extracting data (two: A.B. and G.P.).

elements.quote: Two independent authors (A.B. and G.P.) extracted data on publication year, country, and characteristics of the study population (e.g., age, Injury Severity Score [ISS], systolic blood pressure, heart rate, Glasgow Coma Scale, type of injury [blunt %], type of systemic hemostatic agents, and outcome data) using a standardized data-collection form in a spreadsheet format (Microsoft Excel, Redmond, WA, USA).
elements.reason: It explicitly states the data were extracted by two independent authors.

elements.quote: Discrepancies between reviewers were resolved by consulting a third author (O.C.).
elements.reason: The process for resolving disagreements between reviewers is described (consulting a third author, O.C.).

elements.quote: Authors were contacted if the reported data were insufficient or unclear.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes contacting study authors to obtain/confirm insufficient or unclear data.

elements.quote: using a standardized data-collection form in a spreadsheet format (Microsoft Excel, Redmond, WA, USA).
elements.reason: An automation tool used for data collection is named (Microsoft Excel spreadsheet format), but details on training and validation of the tool are not provided.
No method is reported for translating articles for data collection.
No software is specified for extracting data from figures.

elements.quote: When multiple publications for the same trial reported different outcomes or follow-up data, they were counted as a single publication. Discrepancies between reviewers were resolved by consulting a third author (O.C.).
elements.reason: The manuscript provides decision rules for handling multiple publications for the same trial and resolving reviewer discrepancies, but it does not fully describe decision rules for selecting data from multiple reports beyond these points.

elements.quote: The primary outcome was the overall mortality (at 24 or 48 h or 1 month), while the secondary outcomes were causespecific mortality at 1 month (e.g., multiple organ failure [MOF], head injury, hemorrhage), health-related quality of life; any adverse effect (e.g., MOF); blood product use; mortality at 12 months, hemorrhage expansion; and patientreported outcomes.
elements.reason: Outcome domains/results are listed (overall mortality; cause-specific mortality; health-related quality of life; adverse effects; blood product use; mortality at 12 months; hemorrhage expansion; patient-reported outcomes), but the evidence does not clearly define outcome domains beyond giving examples and listing outcomes.

elements.quote: The primary outcome was the overall mortality (at 24 or 48 h or 1 month), while the secondary outcomes were causespecific mortality at 1 month ... health-related quality of life; any adverse effect ... blood product use; mortality at 12 months, hemorrhage expansion; and patientreported outcomes.
elements.reason: Time points are specified for some outcomes (overall mortality at 24/48 h or 1 month; cause-specific mortality at 1 month; mortality at 12 months), but the measurement time frame is not specified for several other secondary outcomes (e.g., health-related quality of life, adverse effects, blood product use, hemorrhage expansion, patient-reported outcomes).
The evidence does not state whether all compatible results within each outcome domain (e.g., all measures/time points/analyses) were sought.
No information is provided on a process to select results when not all compatible results were sought.
The evidence does not report changes to outcome-domain inclusion, definitions, or importance with rationales.
The evidence does not report changes to processes for selecting results within eligible outcome domains with rationales.
Although the primary outcome is named, the evidence does not state that outcomes “considered most important for interpreting conclusions” were prioritized with a rationale.

elements.quote: Two independent authors (A.B. and G.P.) extracted data on publication year, country, and characteristics of the study population (e.g., age, Injury Severity Score [ISS], systolic blood pressure, heart rate, Glasgow Coma Scale, type of injury [blunt %], type of systemic hemostatic agents, and outcome data) using a standardized data-collection form in a spreadsheet format (Microsoft Excel, Redmond, WA, USA).
elements.reason: The variables/data items sought are listed (e.g., age, ISS, vitals, type of injury, type of agent, outcome data), but the evidence does not show that all variables are explicitly defined.
No explicit description of assumptions made about missing or unclear study information is provided in the retrieved evidence.
Although data were extracted using a 'standardized data-collection form,' the retrieved evidence does not cite any tool used to determine which data items to collect.

elements.quote: The Cochrane risk-of-bias tool was used to evaluate the internal validity of the included RCTs.
elements.reason: The specific risk-of-bias tool is named (Cochrane risk-of-bias tool), but no tool version is reported.
The evidence does not report the domains, components, or items assessed by the risk-of-bias tool.
The evidence does not state whether an overall risk-of-bias judgment was made or the rules used to derive it.
No adaptations to an existing risk-of-bias tool are described in the provided evidence.
No newly developed risk-of-bias tool is described in the provided evidence, so this criterion does not apply based on what is reported.

Although the evidence reports two independent authors for data extraction and a third author for resolving selection disagreements, it does not report how many reviewers assessed risk of bias, their independence for risk-of-bias assessment, or disagreement-resolution procedures.
The evidence mentions contacting authors if reported data were insufficient/unclear, but it does not specify processes to obtain or confirm risk-of-bias information from investigators.
The evidence does not describe any automation tools used for risk-of-bias assessment (including training, performance, or validation).

elements.quote: Treatment effects provided an estimate of the risk ratio (RR) for dichotomized outcomes and a mean difference (MD) or standardized mean difference (SMD) value when different outcome measurements were present for continuous outcomes, along with 95% confidence intervals (CI).
elements.reason: The effect measures used for dichotomous and continuous outcomes in synthesis are explicitly specified (RR for dichotomized outcomes; MD or SMD for continuous outcomes).

elements.quote: For the primary outcome (i.e., mortality) the clinical relevance was assessed with the minimal important differences (MIDs) taken as risk ratios (RRs) of 0.75 and 1.25. For instance, the RR of 0.75 of mortality is taken as the line denoting the boundary between no clinically important effect and a clinically significant benefit, whilst the RR of 1.25 is taken as the line denoting the boundary between no clinically important effect and a clinically significant harm [20].
elements.reason: Thresholds (MIDs expressed as RR 0.75 and 1.25) and their rationale for interpreting clinical relevance for mortality are reported.
No method is described for re-expressing synthesized results using another effect measure (e.g., transforming between RR/OR/MD/SMD), based on the retrieved evidence.

While effect measures are reported, the retrieved evidence does not justify the choice of effect measure beyond the MID interpretation for mortality; no stated justification for selecting RR vs MD/SMD (or other rationale for effect-measure choice) is provided.

elements.quote: Two independent authors (A.B. and G.P.) completed reference screening and study selection using the following predefined inclusion criteria: (1) population : children, young people, or adults who have experienced a suspected hemorrhage or TBI following a traumatic incident; (2) intervention : administration of a systemic hemostatic agent, (e.g., rFVIIa, TXA, fibrinogen concentrate, prothrombin complex concentrate, or another anti-fibrinolytic agent); (3) comparison : no treatment, placebo, standard care (e.g., crystalloids, blood components), or any other hemostatic agent; and (iv) setting: systemic hemostatic treatment initiated in the prehospital setting. Only RCTs were considered eligible for inclusion; case reports, editorials, and letters were excluded from the search. When multiple publications for the same trial reported different outcomes or follow-up data, they were counted as a single publication. Discrepancies between reviewers were resolved by consulting a third author (O.C.).
elements.reason: The review describes how eligibility was decided for study selection, including predefined inclusion/exclusion criteria, that two independent authors performed screening/selection, and how disagreements were resolved.

elements.quote: Authors were contacted if the reported data were insufficient or unclear.
elements.reason: The review reports one approach to handling insufficient/unclear data during extraction (contacting authors), but does not describe other data-preparation methods required for synthesis such as handling missing summary statistics in meta-analysis or data conversions.

elements.quote: Descriptive tables and quantitative analyses for the following outcomes are shown in Supplemental Material 4.
elements.reason: The evidence states that descriptive tables are provided in Supplemental Material 4, but it does not describe the tabular structures used or the specific data included in those tables.

elements.quote: Cause-specific mortality: Bleeding death at 1 month was significantly reduced in patients who received TXA com- pared to placebo, whereas no differences between the groups at 1 month were detected for MOF, head injury, pulmonary embolism, and sepsis (Table S3 and Figs. S3S5 in Supplemental Material 4).
elements.reason: The evidence indicates that figures (Figs. S3S5) accompany the tables in Supplemental Material 4, but it does not describe the graphical methods used (e.g., what types of plots/graphs and how they are constructed).
No evidence reports the basis for ordering or grouping studies within tables or graphs.
No evidence reports any rationale for using non-standard graphs.

elements.quote: The analyses were performed using Review Manager Version 5.4 (Cochrane Collaboration, London, UK).
elements.reason: The statistical software (Review Manager) and its version (5.4) are reported.

elements.quote: General characteristics were descriptively synthesized. When sufficient outcome data were available, cumulative analyses were performed.
elements.reason: A non-meta-analytic approach (descriptive synthesis) is described, and the condition for performing cumulative analyses is stated; however, the specific alternative synthesis/summary method when meta-analysis is not possible and the rationale for that choice are not clearly described.

elements.quote: A pooled estimate was obtained by fitting the DerSimonian and Laird random-effects model [24] when several studies were combined; conversely, a fixed-effects model was applied.
elements.reason: The review specifies when a random-effects model vs fixed-effects model is used, but does not provide a detailed rationale for each model beyond the condition 'when several studies were combined' (and does not link model choice to specific heterogeneity considerations).

elements.quote: Heterogeneity between study-specific estimates was tested using chi-squared statistics and measured with the ­ I 2 index and the Cochran's Q test [22, 23]. A pooled estimate was obtained by fitting the DerSimonian and Laird random-effects model [24] when several studies were combined; conversely, a fixed-effects model was applied.
elements.reason: The statistical methods used for meta-analysis are reported, including the heterogeneity assessment approach and the use of DerSimonian and Laird random-effects (and fixed-effects otherwise).

elements.quote: Heterogeneity between study-specific estimates was tested using chi-squared statistics and measured with the ­ I 2 index and the Cochran's Q test [22, 23].
elements.reason: Methods to identify/quantify statistical heterogeneity are explicitly reported (chi-squared statistics, I², and Cochran’s Q test).

elements.quote: A pooled estimate was obtained by fitting the DerSimonian and Laird random-effects model [24] when several studies were combined; conversely, a fixed-effects model was applied.
elements.reason: A random-effects model is named (DerSimonian and Laird), but the specific between-study variance estimator is not described explicitly beyond referencing the model.
While 95% confidence intervals are mentioned in general, the method used to calculate confidence intervals for the summary effect in random-effects meta-analysis is not specified.
No other random-effects implementation details (e.g., specific handling options) are reported in the provided evidence.
The provided evidence describes frequentist random-effects/fixed-effects models but does not mention Bayesian meta-analysis or priors.
There is no description of methods to account for statistical dependency among multiple estimates from the same study.
No planned syntheses that were considered impossible/inappropriate, nor the reasons for such decisions, are reported in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: Heterogeneity between study-specific estimates was tested using chi-squared statistics and measured with the ­ I 2 index and the Cochran's Q test [22, 23]. ... Subgroup analyses were planned for (1) type of population (e.g., subjects with significant hemorrhage and subjects with TBI); (2) type of injury (e.g., blunt trauma, penetrating trauma); and (3) doses of systemic hemostatic agent when available.
elements.reason: The methods used to explore heterogeneity are described, including statistical heterogeneity tests (I², Cochran’s Q, chi-squared) and planned subgroup analyses.

elements.quote: Subgroup analyses were planned for (1) type of population (e.g., subjects with significant hemorrhage and subjects with TBI); (2) type of injury (e.g., blunt trauma, penetrating trauma); and (3) doses of systemic hemostatic agent when available.
elements.reason: The factors for subgroup analysis are reported (population type, injury type, dose availability), but factor levels are not fully specified and no expected direction of effect modification is stated.
The evidence does not report whether subgroup/heterogeneity analyses used study-level variables, within-study contrasts, or both.
The evidence does not describe methods used to compare subgroup effects.
No informal methods for exploring heterogeneity when meta-analysis was unsuitable are described.
The evidence does not identify whether any heterogeneity analyses were not pre-specified.

No sensitivity analyses are reported. The Methods section describes heterogeneity testing and planned subgroup analyses, but does not describe any sensitivity analyses to assess robustness of the synthesised results.
The evidence provided does not identify any sensitivity analyses, pre-specified or not pre-specified; therefore it also does not state which sensitivity analyses (if any) were not pre-specified.

No methods are described for assessing risk of bias due to missing results in a synthesis (reporting bias). The provided evidence only states that a risk-of-bias tool was used (Cochrane tool), without describing missing-results/reporting-bias assessment methods.
Although the text mentions using the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool, the evidence does not report the assessed domains/items related to missing results nor the process for deriving an overall judgement.
There is no description of any adaptations to a reporting-bias tool for missing results.
No newly developed reporting-bias tool is described, and no public accessibility is reported.

The evidence reports two independent authors for data extraction and that discrepancies in study selection were resolved by a third author, but it does not report the number of reviewers/independence or disagreement-resolution procedures specifically for reporting-bias (missing results) assessment.

This study has some limitations. First, survival bias may be present when patients die before the administration of treatment; thus, the results might not be generalizable across the trauma population [56]. Second, cause-specific mortality can be affected by a subjective and misclassified evaluation (e.g., an in-hospital death for hemorrhage may be caused by hemorrhage and severe TBI [6]). Third, clinical conditions (e.g., cardiac arrest) may have strongly influenced the treatment indication.

Thus, appropriate strategies may reduce these type of biases [56].
